title: SQL: understanding the result
lead: Read five sales, keep qualifying rows, then build the larger questions one clause at a time.
goals: Work through WHERE, GROUP BY, and HAVING step by step
Distinguish inner and outer joins and calculate their result sizes
Use IN and EXISTS with small datasets

sections.title: Start with one table and one condition
sections.html:
A shop asks: “Which sales are at least 30?” Use this original fixture throughout the single-table examples; amounts share one monetary unit.

Sale(id, city, amount)
1 Hanoi 40
2 Hanoi 70
3 Hue   30
4 Hue   90
5 Hue   10

First ask for every row: SELECT * FROM Sale;. FROM names the input table; * asks for all columns. Now keep only large enough sales:

SELECT id, city, amount
FROM Sale
WHERE amount >= 30;

Test the five amounts in order: 40 passes, 70 passes, 30 passes, 90 passes, 10 fails. The surviving rows have IDs 1,2,3,4. SELECT chooses what each surviving output row contains. Replacing its list with city produces Hanoi,Hanoi,Hue,Hue. Repeated cities remain: SQL normally works with a bag, a collection that can contain repeated rows. SELECT DISTINCT city FROM Sale; instead returns Hanoi and Hue once each. Without ORDER BY, output order is not promised.

We have described the required answer without specifying how to read storage. This is SQL's declarative role. The DBMS can choose algorithms, but may not change values or duplicate counts. SQL grew from IBM's relational work in the 1970s and became standardised in the 1980s; the useful distinction here is its role: DDL defines structures, DML queries or changes rows, and DCL controls privileges.

Try: return only IDs of Hue sales worth at least 30.

Use SELECT id FROM Sale WHERE city = 'Hue' AND amount >= 30;. IDs 3 and 4 pass both tests. ID 5 is in Hue but fails the amount test.

Must the DBMS execute SQL in the listed logical clause order?

No. That order explains meaning; a different physical plan is allowed if it preserves the result.

sections.title: When the question needs a total, form groups
sections.html:
Now the shop asks for each city's total, counting only sales worth at least 30, and wants cities whose total exceeds 100. A row condition can reject the sale of 10, but no individual sale contains the city's total. We must first collect the remaining amounts into groups.

SELECT city, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM Sale
WHERE amount >= 30
GROUP BY city
HAVING SUM(amount) > 100
ORDER BY total DESC, city ASC;
StepVisible result
FROMFive Sale rows
WHEREIDs 1,2,3,4; amount 10 removed
GROUP BY cityHanoi: [40,70]; Hue: [30,90]
SUM(amount)Hanoi: 110; Hue: 120
HAVINGBoth totals exceed 100
SELECT and ORDER BY(Hue,120), (Hanoi,110)

AS total names the output column. SUM adds values; COUNT counts, AVG averages, MIN and MAX select extrema. Here Hanoi's AVG is (40+70)/2=55. GROUP BY makes one result per city. Selecting an ungrouped sale ID alongside that total would be ambiguous: which sale should represent the whole group? Use grouping columns or suitable aggregates.

Only now is the full conceptual order useful: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY/aggregates → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. It describes the meaning, not a compulsory physical execution schedule. WHERE changes which amounts enter a total; HAVING decides whether the computed group appears. The slides' early shorthand about aggregates is refined by their later HAVING example.

Try: change WHERE to amount > 50. Does Hue still have total 120?

No. Only 70 and 90 survive. Hanoi totals 70 and Hue totals 90; neither exceeds 100, so HAVING removes both and the final result is empty.

Key takeaway

WHERE filters rows before aggregation; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Changing WHERE changes which numbers enter SUM. Changing HAVING only determines whether an already-computed group appears.

What happens if the example WHERE condition becomes amount > 50?

Only amounts 70 and 90 remain. Both city totals fail HAVING > 100, so the result is empty.

Current explanation scope: official PDF physical pages 13–18 (printed slides 14–19). Numerical fixtures are original teaching examples.

sections.title: A join returns pairs; existence asks whether a pair exists
sections.html:
A different library question needs two tables. This original fixture starts without NULLs or orphan loans:

Member(mid,name)        Borrow(mid,book)
1 An                    1 A
2 Binh                  1 B
3 Chi                   2 C

We want each member's borrowed books. Match on mid, the member identifier:

SELECT M.name, B.book
FROM Member M LEFT JOIN Borrow B ON M.mid = B.mid
ORDER BY M.mid, B.book;

M and B are aliases, short names for the tables in this query. Test An against Borrow: two rows match mid=1, so output (An,A) and (An,B). Binh produces (Binh,C). Chi has no match: LEFT JOIN preserves Chi with (Chi,NULL). NULL marks the missing right-side value. An INNER JOIN would omit Chi. A join returns one row per matching pair, not one row per member.

Now ask only who has borrowed anything:

SELECT M.name FROM Member M
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Borrow B WHERE B.mid = M.mid)
ORDER BY M.mid;

For An the inner condition finds two rows: existence is true once for this Member row. For Binh it finds one: true. For Chi it finds none: false. Output An,Binh. On this NULL-free fixture, IN with the list 1,1,2 tests the same membership. A correlated subquery refers to the current outer M row; this explains meaning without requiring the optimiser to execute it literally once per row.

Extend the fixture by adding Borrow(4,D), with no foreign-key constraint enforced. There is no Member 4. LEFT JOIN still gives four rows. RIGHT JOIN preserves the orphan and gives An/A,An/B,Binh/C,NULL/D. FULL OUTER JOIN keeps both unmatched sides: the three matched pairs plus Chi/NULL and NULL/D, 3+1+1=5 rows. Neither kind removes An's two matches. NATURAL JOIN matches every same-named column; inspect schemas because adding another shared name can change its condition.

Try: An borrows a third book E. How do the LEFT JOIN and EXISTS outputs change?

The LEFT JOIN gains (An,E), becoming five rows in the initial fixture. EXISTS still returns An and Binh: the new loan changes the number of matching pairs, not whether An has any match.

Key takeaway

One left-hand row can produce several result rows. A join produces one row for every matching pair. LEFT JOIN adds a NULL-padded row only when no match exists; it does not limit each member to one row.

Why does the extended FULL OUTER JOIN return five rows?

It has three matched pairs, one unmatched Member and one unmatched Borrow: 3+1+1=5.

sections.title: Control order, then reason about missing values
sections.html:
Return to Sale. “The largest sale” needs an order before a limit:

SELECT id, city, amount FROM Sale
ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC LIMIT 1;

Sorting amounts descending yields IDs 4,2,1,3,5. LIMIT 1 keeps (4,Hue,90). The second key id resolves equal amounts. LIMIT without a sufficient order cannot promise which tied or arbitrary row is chosen; OFFSET 1 would skip the first row before taking the requested count.

For a negative question, use the Member/Borrow fixture: who has no loans? Test NOT EXISTS with the same equality condition as above. An has a match and is rejected; Binh has a match and is rejected; Chi has none and survives. Duplicate loans do not change this test.

SELECT M.name FROM Member M
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Borrow B WHERE B.mid=M.mid)
ORDER BY M.mid;

Only after that ordinary case, add Borrow(NULL,E). NULL means an unknown/missing member ID, not a fourth known number. Equality with NULL does not become true, so Chi still has no match. But M.mid NOT IN (SELECT mid FROM Borrow) now differs: for 3, “3 differs from 1 and 1 and 2 and NULL” has TRUE,TRUE,TRUE,UNKNOWN. The whole condition is UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE. Thus NOT IN returns no Member row here. Members 1 and 2 have decisive matches and are also rejected.

Quantifiers extend this reasoning. For non-NULL amounts [30,90], 50>30 is true and 50>90 is false. So 50 > ANY is true, while 50 > ALL is false. IN corresponds to = ANY; NOT IN to <> ALL. On an empty subquery ANY is false and ALL true; with NULLs and no decisive comparison the outcome can be UNKNOWN. ANY/ALL syntax needs PostgreSQL; the site's SQLite lab supports the IN/EXISTS examples. These NULL details are an explicit supplement to the lecture.

Try: remove the NULL loan again. Which Member does NOT IN return, and why?

Chi. The list is now 1,1,2, so every comparison 3<>value is TRUE. The absence of NULL restores the agreement with NOT EXISTS for these non-NULL member IDs.

With Borrow IDs 1,1,2,NULL, does NOT EXISTS still keep Member 3?

Yes. NULL makes no equality match. NOT IN instead produces UNKNOWN for 3 and WHERE discards it.

quiz.question: In Sale, what is Hue’s total after WHERE amount >= 30?
quiz.explanation: The row with amount=10 is filtered out, leaving 30+90=120. WHERE filters individual rows before GROUP BY computes SUM, so the sale of 10 does not contribute.
